source.title: Common and dissociable neural correlates associated with component processes of inductive reasoning

confidence_rationale: Genuinely two-directional and included for that reason. The component-specific networks (fronto-parietal for identification, striatal-thalamic for extrapolation) support stage non-collapsibility; the COMMON recruitment of left superior parietal lobule/precuneus and left DLPFC across both components is evidence that adjacent stages share substrate rather than being fully separable. Confidence is moderate: peer-reviewed in a strong journal but N=20, a 2011 numerical-induction task, and the shared-substrate finding is exactly the kind of partial collapse ARC-113 must survive.
failure_signatures: Left superior parietal lobule extending into precuneus and left DLPFC were COMMONLY recruited across both rule identification and rule extrapolation, so the two components are not substrate-disjoint; a strict reading of ARC-113 in which stages share no machinery is not supported by this dataset.

The design contrasts rule induction against rule induction WITH application, so extrapolation is never observed in isolation from identification; the component-specific attribution rests on a subtraction, and a genuinely non-decomposable process could produce a similar difference map.

The task is numerical inductive reasoning only; the authors' own framing ties the component decomposition to numerical stimuli, and the paper gives no evidence the same decomposition holds for other rule domains.

mapping.source_claim_statement: The left superior parietal lobule extending into the precuneus and left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were commonly recruited in the two components, while the fronto-parietal network was more specific to identification and the striatal-thalamic network was more specific to extrapolation.
mapping.ree_translation: Rule identification (apprehending a candidate regularity) and rule extrapolation (applying and generalising it) are partially but NOT fully dissociable: they recruit distinct networks on top of a shared prefrontal-parietal core. For ARC-113 this cuts both ways. The component-specific networks support the claim that apprehension and generalisation are distinct stages. The shared core is evidence for the opposing reading -- that stages of the rule pipeline are variations on common machinery rather than architecturally separate modules -- and is the most direct counter-evidence found in this pull.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Shared neural substrate does not by itself refute functional non-collapsibility -- two stages can be computationally distinct while implemented on overlapping tissue, and REE's stages are functional components, not brain regions. So this entry should not be read as strong disconfirmation; it is a warning that a stage-ablation falsifier keyed on SHARED-RESOURCE separability would give the wrong answer. Only two of ARC-113's eleven stages are addressed, in a numerical task, with N=20 in 2011-era fMRI.
mapping.source_context: 20 right-handed adults; event-related fMRI; three conditions -- rule induction (RI), rule induction with application (RIA), and a perceptual judgment control; numerical inductive reasoning.

confidence_components.notes: Peer-reviewed NeuroImage study with an explicit common-vs-dissociable contrast, which is precisely the question ARC-113 poses; capped by small N, single task domain, and the subtraction logic underlying component attribution.
